list.listitem: Acute lower GI bleeding ranges from minor bleeding to life-threatining haemorrhage. B
Diverticulosis is by far the most common cause of lower GI bleeding
Assess the patient's hemodynamic status and initiate resuscitation if needed at the time of initial evaluation and assessment. A
In haemodynamically unstable (HR/SBP > 1) patients, CTA should be considered as initial diagnostic study, which can detect > 0.3 ml/min rates of bleeding. Treat endoscopically if possibleB
If the CTA is negative, upper GI endoscopy should be consdiered to rule out an upper GI source of bleeding.

Colonoscopy should be considered in all patinets before discharge to determine the source of the bleeding. However, it might not needed if bleeding subsided and < 12 month high quality colonescopy was done and showed diverticular bleed without evidence of neoplasm. B
Patients who are stable (HR/SBP < 1) and at low risk for complications by a validated risk score may be considered for outpatient evaluation.C

After initial resuscitation, therapy consists of transfusion if necessary, reversal of anticoagulation, and definitive therapy to stop bleeding (eg, surgical, vasopressin, embolization, thermal contact, band ligation, epinephrine injection). B

background.definition: Lower GI bleeding (LGIB) is defined as bleeding emanating from a source distal to the ligament of Treitz.

list.listitem: The overall incidence of LGIB is believed to range between 33 and 87 of 100,000; however, high-quality epidemiologic studies in LGIB are lacking.
The incidence increases from 1 per 100,000 in the third decade of life to 200 per 100,000 in the ninth decade, with the average age being 66 to 73 years.
Men are affected significantly more than women.
LGIB is one-fifth as common as upper GI bleed.

Aspirin, NSAIDs and P2Y12 inhibitors shown to increase the risk of new diverticular bleed. Among veterans elderly patients who are on complex antithrombotic therapy the incidence of LGIB is 70.1/1000 patient-years with numbers-needed-to-harm found to be 15-23 per year.
LGIB is one of the most common GI indications for hospitlization.
LGIB accounts for 24% of all GI bleeding events.
The overall mortality from a lower GI bleed is approximately 2% to 4%.
LGIB shows a high rebleeding rate of 13%–19% even after successfully control with endoscopy.

The most common causes include diverticular bleeding with an incidence as high as 66%, followed by hemorrhoids (21%), ischemic colitis (12.9%), neoplasia (8%), infectious colitis (5%), inflammatory bowel disease (4%) & angiodysplasia (2%). Other causes include radiation protctitis, small intestinal bleeding and iatrogenic - post-polypectomy bleeds.
Massive upper GI bleeding can present as hematochezia in up to15% of the patients and often associated with hemodynamic unstability.
The source of LGIB remains unidentifed in about 15-25%
The use of antithrombotic drugs and anticoagulants significantly increases the risk of LGIB.

Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) have a similar risk of major GIB compared with traditional anticoagulation; however, dabigatran and rivaroxaban particularly have an increased risk of GIB compared with warfarin and other DOACs Risk factors for GI bleeding events include concommitant aspirin use, baseline anemia and a history of GI bleeding
Concurrent use of NSAIDs and SSRI increase risk of GI bleeding.

Although resumption of antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs after an acute GI bleed has been associated with an increased rebleeding risk, it has been shown that there is a significant reduction in vascular events/death which supports early re-introduction of these agents.
Diverticular bleeding: colonic wall weakness results in saclike protrusion that bleeds due to repeated trauma to the vasa recta.
Hemorrhodis bleeding: engorged and swollen vessels in the anorectal cushions that often leads to painless bleeding.

Ischemic colitis: the colon is predisposed to ischemia due to its poor collateral circulation, low blood flow, and high bacteria count. Any event or condition that compromises colonic blood flow may result in ischemic insult. The watershed areas of the splenic flexure, rectosigmoid junction, and right colon are more commonly involved because of their particularly tenuous blood supply.
GI vascular ectasias: thought to be the degenerative lesions of the submucosal venules.
Infectious colitis: certain infectious organisms can result in bloody diarrhea including Escherichia coli O157:H7, Salmonella, Clostridiodes difficile, Campylobacter, Yersinia, and Cytomegalovirus.
Neoplasm: due to the overlying erosions or ulcerations.

DOACs have not been shown to increase the risk of new-onset diverticular hemorrhage when compared with antiplatelets. However, patients who experience new-onset LGIB after initiation of oral anticoagulants may be more likely to be subsequently diagnosed with colorectal cancer, hence the importance of up-to-date colon cancer screening before initiation of these drugs or shortly thereafter if it was not done prior to initiation
Use a validated clinical decision rule to risk stratify patients and assist in decisions about discharge and follow-up (see "Clinical decision rules" below). B
Patients who are stable (HR/SBP < 1) and at low risk for complications by a validated risk score may be considered for outpatient evaluation.C
Use CT angiography in patients who are unstable (HR/SBP > 1) with active, persistent bleeding or if endoscopic evaluation is nondiagnostic.C
Non urgent colonoscopy is the recommended initial study for most patients.B

Perform upper GI endoscopy to rule out an upper GI source of bleeding in any patient with melena or if UGI bleed is clinically suspected. It may be the initial study for patients with hematechezia who are unstable and in whom UGI source is considered likely.B

Risk startification with an electronic healthcare record-based machine learning model is promising as it identifes very low risk patients more than the existing scores that potentially decrease unnecessary hospitalizations, yet it is not part of the guidlines.

Differential.Differential_Features: Usually painless bleeding may be accompanied by mild crampy abdominal pain due to colonic spasm from intraluminal blood
Bleeding may be episodic and self-limited. Bleeding is usually venous in origin so it tends to be less massive than diverticular bleeding
Usually associated with abdominal pain. May be associated with fever
Usually low grade and with recurrent bleeding; may have history of weight loss and altered bowel habits
May have tenesmus and history of constipation; examination may reveal anal tags or hemorrhoids
Recurrent, painless, bright red bleeding in a child; may present with intestinal obstruction - abdominal pain, nausea & vomiting

Differential.Differential_Name: Rare: solitary rectal ulcer syndrome, colonic varices, Dieulafoy's lesions, portal hypertension-induced enteropathy, prostate biopsy site, endometriosis

list.listitem: A focused history, physical examination, and laboratory evaluation should be obtained at the time of patient presentation to assess the severity of bleeding, its possible location and the etiology. Initial patient assessment and hemodynamic resuscitation should be performed simultaneously.

Take a focused history regarding the nature and duration of bleeding including stool color and frequency along with associated symptoms like abdominal pain, tenesmus/urgency, change in bowel habits, fever, or weight loss.

Review past medical history including previous bleeding episodes, trauma, past abdominal surgeries, history of inflammatory bowel disease, history of radiation therapy to the abdomen and pelvis, and past history of major organ dysfunction (including cardiopulmonary, renal, and liver disease).
Obtain history of medication use (including NSAIDS, aspirin, and anticoagulants) and allergies.
Determine whether there is any history of chest pain/palpitations, dyspnea at rest or on exertion, light-headedness, or postural symptoms suspicious for large volume of blood loss.

Perform physical examination including vital signs and orthostatic BP. A drop of more than 20 mm Hg or an increase of more than 30 beats/min in pulse is strong evidence in favor of moderate or large acute blood loss. Marked tachycardia and tachypnea, associated with hypotension and depressed mental status, is indicative of blood loss of more than 1500 mL (30% circulatory blood volume).
Perform cardiopulmonary, abdominal, and digital rectal (DRE) examination.

Bowel symptoms most strongly associated with colorectal cancer include rectal bleeding (LR+ 8.5), abdominal pain (LR+ 3.4), weight loss (2.7) and the combination of rectal bleeding and anemia (LR+ 8.3).Among patients with abdominal pain, palpatory tenderness in the LLQ is strongly associated with a diagnosis of acute diverticulitis.

The likelihood of serious colorectal disease (either cancer or inflammatory bowel disease) is increased in patients without abdominal pain (LR+ 2.1), rectal blood loss (LR+ 1.7), abnormal digital rectal (LR+ 1.7), absence of abdominal bloating (LR+ 1.5) and rectal mucus (LR+ 1.5).

British guidelines (2021) and ACG guidelines (2023) both recommend CT angiography as the initial study in patients who are unstable (shock index (HR/SBP) >= 1) given its high sensitivity (90%) and specificity (92%), followed by treatment of any identified lesions either with interventional radiology or endoscopically if possible. Patients with negative CT angiography should proceed to lower and possibly upper endoscopic evaluation.

Colonoscopy diagnostic accuracy ranges from 72% to 86% in the setting of LGIB. It is recommended as the initial study for most patients by ACG guidelines as It is safe and has low morbidity and mortality. It allows precise localization of the bleeding source for potential therapeutic intervention. If colonic source not found, the use of a transparent clear cap during colonoscopy and intubation of terminal ileum to exclude a proximal source of bleeding shown to improve diagnostic accuracy Patients who undergo colonoscopy have a shorter length of stay compared with those who do not.Patients who have had a recent colonoscopy within 12 months with adequate bowel preparation showing diverticulosis and no colorectal neoplasia, can be potentially be managed conservatively without performing a colonoscopy if bleeding subsides while in hospital.
EGD is recommended for patients with melena and in whom UGI source is otherwise clinically suspected.

Both observational data and data from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) show no significant difference in re-bleeding rates when comparing early colonoscopy (within 24 hours of presentation) with elective colonoscopy (after 24 hours) for patients admitted to the hospital with LGIB.This supports the practice of non-urgent inpatient colonoscopy as studies have shown that urgent colonoscopy (within 24 hours) does not improve clinical outcomes i.e. rebleeding and mortality

Nuclear scans require GI bleeding at a rate of 0.1 mL/min or more for localization. Nuclear scans are either technetium sulfur colloid or technetium-labeled red blood cells. Early scanning is recommended to identify potential bleeding sites. These studies are difficult to interpret, have poor accuracy in identifying the bleeding site, and poorly predict subsequent angiogram results.

Nuclear scans are only recommended in rare cases where CTA is unavailable or contraindicated (high concern for contrast induced nephropathy) due to widespread availability of CTA and the limitations of nuclear scans ( long study duration and inability to precisely locate the bleeding site).

Consider small bowel evaluation if no source of bleeding is identified on colonoscopy and upper endoscopy is negative. Push enteroscopy provides examination of the proximal 60 to 80 cm of the jejunum.

Capsule endoscopy is a simple, noninvasive way to study the small bowel, with a diagnostic yield as high as 92% in obscure GI bleeding. An ACG guideline recommends it as the first-line procedure for small bowel investigation. Capsule endoscopy is more sensitive and specific than push enteroscopy in identifying bleeding sources within the small bowel, although it does not permit biopsies to be taken.

In a case series of patients with obscure GI bleeding, double balloon endoscopy of the small intestine was helpful in determining the source of bleeding with diagnostic rates for patients with overt-ongoing, overt-previous, and occult bleeding of 100.0%, 48.4% and 42.1%, respectively.
Helical CT is useful for diagnosing colonic angiodysplasia if abnormal (LR+ 70).

The decision to manage patients as outpatients can be based of several decision rules. However these decision tools should supplement not replace clinician judgment. They help identify patients who are low-risk for requiring hospital-based interventions; Low-risk patients who do not have ongoing bleeding and who have had a recent, high-quality colonoscopy showing diverticulosis and excluding etiologies such as colorectal neoplasia may be discharged early from the hospital with outpatient follow-up, thereby avoiding potentially unnecessary inpatient colonoscopy

AIMs-65 and RS scores are the strongest in predicting death. Oakland score is the strongest in detecting rebleeding and blood transfusion, a score of < 9 is associated with a 95% chance of safe discharge.
Strate score is the most discriminative predictor of the need for hemostasis.
The Strate clinical rule helps guide the initial triage of patients with LGIB and it helps predict outcomes, and thus is a more standardized and cost-effective approach to this disorder (see ).
A second well-validated clinical rule for patients with any GI bleed is based on age, presence of comorbidities, blood pressure, and heart rate.
The ABC score predicts mortality in both upper and lower GI bleed.
Initiate resuscitation efforts concurrently with the initial evaluation of the patient to prevent complications of blood loss.

Initial laboratory studies should include CBC, serum electrolytes, BUN, and creatinine. Coagulation studies, the blood type and cross match for possible transfusion, and an ECG for patients who are unstable or with major bleeding should also be obtained.

British guidelines (2021) classify patients as unstable (shock index of HR/SBP >= 1) or stable. If unstable, CT angiography is the initial recommended test followed by endoscopic or interventional radiology intervention to treat any bleeding sites. If CT angiography is negative, patients should undergo lower and if indicated upper endoscopic evaluation. Patients who are stable should be classified based on their risk of complications using the Oakland or Strate risk scores. Patients at low risk for complications may be considered for outpatient evaluation while those at high risk should be hospitalized and undergo urgent lower and possibly upper endoscopy.

ACG guidelines (2023) recommend non urgent colonoscopy as the inital study for most patients. Updated guidelines do not recommend that it has to be in the first 24 hours. Upper endoscopy should be considered as the initial study for patients with hematochezia who are hemodynamically unstable. For patients who are unstable and would not tolerate prep and colonoscopy, CT angiography is recommended as the initial study.

Assess patients hemodynamic status and initiate resuscitation if needed at the time of the initial evaluation and assessment, including transfusion if hemoglobin <= 7 g/dl or patient is hemodynamically unstable.C
In hemodynamically stable patients, colonoscopy is the first-line diagnostic and therapeutic intervention. C
Endoscopic therapies such as clipping, band ligation and coagulation are indicated when active or recent stigmata of bleeding are detected.B
Vasopressin infusion and embolization can be performed during arteriography and colonoscopy for management of colonic diverticular bleeding. B
Use thermal contact modalities and epinephrine injection for bleeding diverticula, vascular ectasia, or post-polypectomy bleeding sites. B

Tranexamic acid did not reduce death from gastrointestinal bleeding but was associated with a higher rate of venous thromboembolism in patients admitted with significant upper or lower gastrointestinal bleeding. It was also associated with increase risk of seizures.. ACG guidelines (2023) specifically recommend against using antifibrinolytic agents including tranexamic acid.

Reversal of anticoagulation is recommended in patients with life threatening LGIB not responding to initial resuscitation and cessation of the anticoagulant alone especially if INR is above the therapeutic range. 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) for VKA reversal, (idarucizumab for dabigatran and andexanet alfa for apixaban and rivaroxaban. Resumption of anticoagultaion after cessation of LGIB is recommended given that resumption of anticoagulation decreases risk of thromboembolism and mortality.post bleeding

Continuation of low dose aspirin for secondary prevention during hospitalization is recommended if possible. Nonaspirin antiplatelets should be imitially put on hold in patients with severe hematochezia. In patients with recent cardiac stents (within 1 year), the decision to temporarily hold antiplatelets should use a multidisciplinary approach. Discontinue non-aspirin NSAIDs and aspirin for primary ASCD prevention after hospitalization for diverticular hemorrhage. However, aspirin for established ASCVD should be continued given the benefits of reducing future ischemic events. Re-evaluation of risks vs benefits of continuing non-aspirin antiplatelets such as P2Y12 receptor antagonists in a multidisciplinary setting is helpful.

A RCT of 2621 older patients with atrial fibrillation living with frailty (≥75 years of age plus a Groningen Frailty Indicator score ≥3) were randomly assigned to switch from international normalized ratio-guided VKA treatment to an NOAC or to continued VKA treatment. Switching was associated with clinically significant more bleeding complications compared with continuing VKA treatment, without an associated reduction in thromboembolic complications.
Surgical option should be undertaken only once all interventional radiologic and endoscopic measures have been exhausted.
Accurate presurgical localization of the bleeding site improves postoperative morbidity and mortality.
Surgery is useful after the third flare of diverticulitis.

Endoscopic hemostasis using clipping, themal measures or band ligation is the preferred approach to controlling identified bleeding sites although head to head trials are lacking. For unstable patients with a site identified using CT angiography, interventional radiology is also an option.
The specific modality (mechanical, injection, or thermal) depends on the site and etiology of bleeding, and of the gastroenterologist's experience with that modality.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of six studies (two randomized controlled trials and four observational studies) of 23,419 patients with acute lower gastrointestinal bleeing (LGIB); concluded that urgent colonscopy (9,498 patients) was associated with simliar outcomes compared to elective colonscopy (13,921 patients) with regard to mortality, rebleeding or requirements for surgery. Some studies have demonstrated that urgent colonoscopy is associated with a shorter course of hospitalization (<7 days), whereas others have found no difference in the rates of rebleeding.
Transcatheter arterial embolization is emerging as a newer modality when endoscopic hemostasis fails; it is a minimally invasive alternative to surgical intervention.

In cases of refractory LGIB, UI-EWD hemostatic powder demonstrated a remarkable success rate in achieving hemostasis, while also exhibiting promising outcomes in reducing the re-bleeding rate within a 30-day period. Particularly, UI-EWD exhibits a favorable safety profile across all segments of the colon.

The goal of transfusion should be to minimize the risk of complications due to red blood cell loss and to correct coagulopathy but should not be used to transfuse to an arbitrary level of hemoglobin/hematocrit.

ACG guidelines (2023) recommend transfusion with packed RBCs to maintain a hemoglobin > 7 g/dl. For patients with massive bleeding or comorbid cardiovascular disease a threshold of 8 g/dl should be used

British guidelines (2021) recommend a trigger of 7 g/dl and a target of 7 to 9 g/dl post-transfusion. Trigger and target of 8 g/dl and 10 g/dl respectively should be used for patients with comorbid cardiovascular disease.

A coagulopathy (PT/INR >1.5) or thrombocytopenia (<50,000/microliter) should be corrected, if possible with fresh-frozen plasma and platelet transfusions, respectively. The ideal hematocrit depends on the patient's age, the rate of bleeding, and the presence of comorbid conditions (eg, coronary artery disease [CAD], emphysema, or cirrhosis). A hematocrit of 20% to 25% may be acceptable for a young patient without other significant problems, but could be detrimental for elderly patients with CAD. Maintaining the hematocrit around 30% for high-risk patients is recommended. The volume of transfusion of red blood cells and blood products must be individualized.
Administered platelets to maintain a platelet count of .30x109 /L, and a higher threshold of 50x109 /L can be considered if endoscopic procedures are required.
Up to 75% of diverticular bleeding episodes resolve without interventions.

Vasopressin infusion and embolization can be performed via the catheter during arteriography and colonoscopy for management of colonic diverticular bleeding, and is the preferred first-line approach. Up to 91% of patients receiving intra-arterial vasopressin will stop bleeding, but as many as 50% will rebleed on cessation of vasopressin. In these patients however, vasopressin will permit semielective surgery. The vasopressin infusion begins at a rate of 0.2 U/min with repeat angiography after 20 minutes. If bleeding persists, the rate is increased to 0.4 to 0.6 U/min; if bleeding is controlled, the infusion is continued, in an intensive care unit setting, for 24 to 36 hours and then tapered over 24 hours.

Thermal contact modalities, including heat probe and bipolar/multipolar coagulation, and/or epinephrine injection, can be used in the treatment of bleeding diverticula, vascular ectasia, or post-polypectomy bleeding sites.

Endoscopic band ligation or endoscopic detachable snare ligation have recently emerged as advances in the management of colonic diverticular bleeding with a decrease in <30 day and even 1 year rebleeding rate and have even been shown to eliminate the target diverticulum.

High-dose barium enema is thought to prevent diverticular bleeding by both tamponade on the bleeding vessel and by a direct hemostatic effect. A recent small RCT of 54 patients randomized to 800 mg barium via an enema delivered in 400 mL of tap water was associated with a 1-year bleeding rate of 15% vs 43% in those randomized to conservative treatment.
In patients with bleeding from angiodysplasia who received endoscopic therapy, the rate of recurrent bleeding after 22 months was 34%.
Somatostatin analogues (octreotide) in treating angiodysplasic bleeding was associated with a 14.5 times higher odds of bleeding cessation than comparison interventions.

In a recent RCT showed octreotide treatment effectively reduces transfusion requirements and healthcare utilization of patients with angiodysplasia-related anemia, significantly increasing patients’ quality of life after they fail 1 endoscopic attempt.
A meta-analysis of 7 studies showed that thalidomide is an option for refractory LGIB as it was associated with higher odds of bleeding cessation, but more adverse effects.
In patients with Heyde's syndrome (aortic stenosis associated with colonic angiodyslpasia), aortic valve replacement decreased the rate of re-bleeding by 81% among patients with GI hemorrhage.
Hospitalize all patients with acute LGIB for their workup and appropriate management.

The most important potential complication from acute LGIB is hemodynamic instability. The emphasis should be on assessing the patient's volume status and resuscitating the patient aggressively as needed.

In patients bleeding due to the direct thrombin inhibitor dabigatran, the monoclonal antibody idarucizumab is associated with improved measures of clotting (ie, the thrombin time and the ecarin clotting time) in 88% to 98% of patients with either active uncontrolled bleeding or requiring urgent anticoagulant reversal due to planned surgery. However a small percentage of these patients experienced a thrombotic event.

In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 studies, the pooled prevalence of post-colonoscopy complications were 0.5/1000 for perforation, 2.6/1000 for bleeding, and 2.9/10,000 for mortality, complication rates in 2015 were similar to or better than the rates calculated for 2001.
Recent studies have shown that use of clips to close mucosal defects after resection of large colonic lesions have been associated with a decreased risk of delayed bleeding.
LGIB is self-limited in 80% of patients. B
A clinical rule can also help assess prognosis (). B
Only 1% of patient younger than 40 with nonacute rectal bleeding have cancer.

A retrospective analysis of 1644 patients with GI hemorrhage and a measured lactate level concluded that a lactate level >4 mmol/L was associated with a six-fold increase in the risk of in-hospital mortality.
80% of LGIB will stop spontaneously.
A systematic review similarly concluded that colonic diverticular bleeding will stop spontaneously in 80% of patients; rebleeding occurs in 25% of patients over 73 months.
Identification of the bleeding source is challenging, and rebleeding can occur in 25% of patients.
Hypovolemic shock, blood transfusion during admission and hyperlipidemia have emerged as predictors of recurrent bleeding and readmission within 90 days.
If the need for blood transfusion within the first 24 hours is more than 4 U, the patient has a 50% chance of requiring surgery.
A clinical decision rule (see ) exists to help determine the prognosis of lower GI bleed.

A clinical tool with eight variables (age, dementia, metastatic cancer, chronic kidney disease, chronic pulmonary disease, anticoagulant use, admission hematocrit, and albumin) had been validated in predicting 30-day mortality in patients hospitalized with lower gastrointestinal bleeding.
Mortality from LGIB is 5% or less, but it can reach 23% if bleeding occurred after hospitalization.
In patients who receive more than 2 U of blood, mortality increases to 15%.
1% of patients younger than 40 with nonacute rectal bleed have cancer.
In patients with advanced risk for colorectal carcinoma, like those with a history of adenomatous polyps or inflammatory bowel disease, perform follow-up colonoscopy according to guidelines.
Similarly, perform colonoscopy every 3 to 5 years in patients over the age of 50 with recurrent bleeding.

A retrospective study found the majority of patients who present to the outpatient clinic for rectal bleed, fail to complete the recommanded follow-up workup, mainly due to either not having the procedure ordered or scheduled.
Encourage patients to eat a high-fiber diet, especially those with diverticular disease.
Perform regular screening colonoscopies.
LGIB is more common in older patients.
70% of patients with LGIB have at least one comorbid condition that increases their risk for adverse outcome; such patients need more attention.
Hemorrhoids are a common cause of hematochezia in pregnant patients.
Meckel's diverticulum is a more common cause of LGIB in younger patients.

feature.caption: Clinical Decision Rule for Prognosis of Lower GI Bleed.
feature.feature_body:
Sign or Symptom Points
Heart rate ≥100/min 1
Systolic blood pressure ≤115 mmHg 1
Syncope 1
Nontender abdominal examination 1
Bleeding in the first 4 hours of evaluation 1
Aspirin use 1
>2 active comorbid conditions (from Charlson Index)a 1
Total:
Points Probability of Severe Lower GI bleed (%)
>3 84
1-3 43
0 9
aCharlson ME, Pompei P, Ales KL, MacKenzie CR. A new method of classifying prognostic comorbidity in longitudinal studies: development and validation. J Chronic Dis 1987;40:373-383. Data also from Strate LL, Orav EJ, Syngal S. Early predictors of severity in acute lower intestinal tract bleeding. Arch Intern Med 2003;163:838-843.
